newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Strike hits hard in S.Africa's Eastern Cape.
newsitem.headline: Strike hits hard in S.Africa's Eastern Cape.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union federation began a week of protests over disputed employment legislation on Monday, hitting hard in the economically depressed Eastern Cape.
The 1.9-million member Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) chose the Eastern Cape province, home to the country's automobile industry, to start four days of regional strikes.

Regional business groups estimated lost turnover of 117.1 million rand ($25 million) and chamber of commerce chief Kevin Wakeford said around 90 percent of Cosatu members, or 70 percent of the total workforce, did not arrive for work in the greater Port Elizabeth-Uitenhage area.
The strike hit automobile manufacturing and ancillary sectors, including engineering, textiles and tyres, he said.
Buses and taxis were not running in the metropolitan region, the economic hub of the province.
Wakeford said lost wages had been estimated at around 23.6 million rand, and he estimated a loss of 60 million rand in contribution to gross domestic product.
Cosatu has organised the four days of action to add pressure to its demands over proposed changes to labour laws, enshrined in the Basic Conditions of Employment bill.
It wants six months' maternity leave for workers, four with pay, and a 40-hour working week to be phased in over five years.
Business has agreed to reduce the working week by an hour to 45 hours, but refuses to commit itself to a 40-hour week.
Employers' groups have argued that some of the bill's provisions could raise employment costs, deterring job creation.
Umbrella group Business South Africa negotiator Adrian du Plessis called for a resumption of negotiations and said the strike campaign would not help to end the impasse over the proposed law.
"The issues are very difficult and I must confess the parties are deeply divided," he told state radio.
"But the proposed programme of protest action has not helped in bringing the parties together at all. If anything it has hardened the attitudes on both sides of the table, rather than softened them."
Cosatu spokeswoman Nowetu Mpati told Reuters there was no reason to resume already prolonged talks with business, since no new proposals had been made.
"We don't have time to waste... We would like this bill to go to parliament this year," she said.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni has repeatedly said the employment bill cannot become law this year unless broad consensus is reached between business and labour in time for its presentation to parliament on September 15.
